# Tabla Suite Specification (`readme_Fluid_Indian_Percussion.md`)
============================================================
## Studio-Grade Indian Classical & Contemporary Tabla Suite
**Instrument:** Tabla (Bayān Bass Drum & Dayān Treble Drum)  
**Traditions:** Hindustani Classical, Khayal, Thumri, Ghazal, Sufi, Bollywood, World Fusion  
**Tuning Class:** Chromatic Melodic Percussion (Dayan Tuned to Song's Tonic $Sa$)  
**Standard Bank / Preset:** Bank 41 Presets 0–11 (Tuned Sa=C..B), Preset 116 (Sa=C#) | GM Drum Kit: Bank 128 Preset 116  
**Multi-Velocity Layers:** 3 Tiers (Soft `0-60`, Medium `61-110`, Hard `111-127`)

---

## 1. Instrument Physics & Acoustic Character
The Tabla is the centerpiece of North Indian classical rhythm. It consists of two complementary drums:
* **Bayān (Left Drum / Dagga):** Deep kettle drum made of heavy polished brass, copper, or clay. Struck with the flat palm or sliding wrist heel. Produces singing, resonant, pitch-bending bass tones (*Ge, Ghasit, Meend*) and dry flat palm slaps (*Ke, Ka*).
* **Dayān (Right Drum / Tabla):** Heavy carved rosewood or sheesham barrel drum with high-tension goatskin and a dense permanent black center paste (*syahi* made of iron dust, boiled rice, and soot). Produces crystalline ringing bell tones (*Tin, Tun*), crisp outer rim snaps (*Na, Ta*), and dry staccato taps (*Te, Ti*).

### Harmonic Architecture
When the Dayan is struck on its rim (*Na*) or center sur (*Tin*), the syahi creates pure, harmonic overtone spectra resembling a singing pitch. Always tune or pitch the Dayan to match the root key ($Sa$) of your song.

---

## 3. Idiomatic Patterns for AI Arrangers

### A. Classic 8-Matra Keherwa Theka (4/4 Meter — 2 Bars = 8 Beats)
Tempo: 85 – 125 BPM  
*Note: Sam (Matra 1) is heavily accented with Dha. Matra 5 is the unaccented Khali (open Ta without bass).*
```
Matra:   1  .   2  .   3  .   4  .   5  .   6  .   7  .   8  .
Bol:    Dha .  Ge  .  Na  .  Tin .  Ta  .  Ka  .  Dhin .  Na  .
Note:   60  .  36  .  48  .  50  .  48  .  38  .  62   .  48  .
Vel:   120  .  85  .  95  .  80  .  85  .  90  . 110   .  85  .
```

### B. High-Energy Lyrical / Ghazal Keherwa (with Meends & Syncopation)

```

Bol:    Dha  . SldGe .  Na  Tin  .  Tu  Ta   .  Ka  Chhit Dhin .  Na  .
Note:   60   .  39   .  48  50   .  53  48   .  38   52   62   .  48  .
Vel:   122   . 100   .  95  85   .  80  90   .  95   90  112   .  85  .
```

### C. Classical 16-Matra Teental (4/4 Meter — 4 Bars = 16 Beats)
Tempo: 70 – 140 BPM  
*Structure: 4 Vibhags (4 + 4 + 4 + 4). Tali on Matras 1, 5, 13; Khali on Matra 9 (Tin Tin Ta Ta).*
```
Vibhag 1 (Sam):    1.0 Dha (125)   2.0 Dhin (100)   3.0 Dhin (95)    4.0 Dha (105)
Vibhag 2 (Tali):   5.0 Dha (110)   6.0 Dhin (95)    7.0 Dhin (95)    8.0 Dha (100)
Vibhag 3 (Khali):  9.0 Dha (85)   10.0 Tin  (80)   11.0 Tin  (80)   12.0 Ta  (85)
Vibhag 4 (Tali):  13.0 Ta  (105)  14.0 Dhin (100)  15.0 Dhin (100)  16.0 Dha (115)
```

### D. 7-Matra Roopak Taal (@TIMESIG 7/8 — 1 Bar = 3.5 Beats)
Tempo: 80 – 120 BPM  
*Structure: 3 + 2 + 2. Begins uniquely on Khali (Tin Tin Na).*
```
Matra:   1    2    3    | 4    5    | 6    7
Bol:    Tin  Tin  Na    | Dhe  Na   | Dhe  Na
Note:   50   50   48    | 62   48   | 62   48
Vel:    85   80   90    | 115  90   | 110  90
```

### E. 6-Matra Dadra Taal (3/4 or 6/8 Meter)
Tempo: 100 – 160 BPM  
*Structure: 3 + 3 (Dha Dhin Na | Dha Tin Na).*
```
Matra:   1     2     3     | 4     5     6
Bol:    Dha   Dhin  Na     | Dha   Tin   Na
Note:   60    62    48     | 60    50    48
Vel:   120   105    90     | 105   80    85
```

---

## 4. LMP Implementation Rules & AI Best Practices

When composing or modifying Tabla tracks in LMP:
1. **Track Header:**
   ```lmp
   @TRACK 4 Indian_Tabla
   @CHANNEL 10
   @SF2 Fluid_Indian_Percussion
   ```
2. **Minimal @MAP Declarations:**
   Declare **only** the strokes actually used in the track to keep code clean and token-efficient:
   ```lmp
   @MAP Dha=60
   @MAP Dhin=62
   @MAP Ge=36
   @MAP Na=48
   @MAP Tin=50
   @MAP Ka=38
   ```
3. **Dynamic Contrast (Crucial for Realism):**
   * **Sam Accent (Beat 1):** Always set velocity to `115–125`.
   * **Khali (Unstressed section):** Keep velocity to `70–85` and use *Ta* (48) or *Ka* (38) without open *Ge*.
   * **Ghost Notes / Taps:** Center taps (*Te*, *Re*) should sit at `55–75`.
4. **Duration & Articulation:**
   * Keep percussive note durations between `0.25` and `0.5` beats.
   * For rapid *tirakita* rolls, use duration `0.125` to `0.25` beats with alternating strokes (*Te* 52, *Re* 54, *Ke* 38, *Ta* 48).

# Dholak Studio Specification (`readme_Dholak.md`)
==================================================
## Authentic Indian Folk, Qawwali, Ghazal & Bollywood Percussion
**Instrument:** Dholak (North Indian Folk Double-Headed Barrel Drum)  
**Traditions:** Qawwali, Ghazal, Bengali Lokgeeti, Punjabi Folk, Bollywood Filmi, Bhajans  
**Tuning Class:** Relative Folk / Natural Body Resonance (Unpitched Treble Skin)  
**Standard Bank / Preset:** Bank 41 Preset 117 (`Dholak Studio`) | GM Drum Kit: Bank 128 Preset 117  
**Multi-Velocity Layers:** 3 Tiers (Soft `0-60`, Medium `61-110`, Hard `111-127`)

---

## 1. Instrument Physics & Acoustic Character
The Dholak is the pulse of subcontinental popular and folk music. Unlike the classical Tabla, its heads lack the dense iron-compound *syahi* application.
* **Left Head (Dhumma / Bass):** Larger diameter, tuned loose. Often has a simple inner tar or resin paste (*masala*) applied inside to lower pitch, producing an energetic, bouncy, pumpy bass tone (*Dhum / Ge*) and loose palm slaps (*Ka*).
* **Right Head (Chhati / Treble):** High-tension goatskin stretched over a wooden hoop. Produces dry, piercing, unpitched cracks (*Chhit*), crisp rim snaps (*Ta*), and singing overtones (*Tin*).

### Why Choose Dholak Over Tabla?
* **Rhythmic Drive:** Dholak has immediate transient attack and fast decay, preventing muddy bass in up-tempo folk and Qawwali grooves.
* **Acoustic Pocket:** Sits naturally under acoustic rhythm guitars, harmonium, and group clapping without clashing with bass guitars.

---

# Khol Studio Specification (`readme_Khol.md`)
================================================
## Sacred Percussion of Bengal (Mridanga of Gaudiya Vaishnava Kirtan & Baul)
**Instrument:** Khol / Mridanga (Terracotta Asymmetrical Clay Drum)  
**Traditions:** Gaudiya Kirtan, Baul Folk, Rabindra Sangeet, Nazrul Geeti, Bengali Lokgeeti  
**Tuning Class:** Chromatic Melodic Percussion (Tuned to Singer's Tonic $Sa$)  
**Standard Bank / Preset:** Bank 43 Presets 0–11 (Tuned Sa=C..B), Preset 116 (Sa=C#) | GM Kit: Bank 128 Preset 118  
**Multi-Velocity Layers:** Natural Dynamic Range with Microtonal Modulation

---

## 1. Instrument Physics & Acoustic Character
The Khol is made of baked earthenware (clay) with a distinctive tapered conical shape.
* **Left Head (Belly / Ghet):** Wide bulbous body tuned very deep. Striking the clay belly creates a hollow, cavernous, organic bass bloom (*Ghet / Ge*) found in no wooden or metal drum.
* **Right Head (Treble Face / Ta):** Extremely small diameter ($< 4	ext{ inches}$) stretched to very high tension with thick black syahi paste. Produces a piercing, silvery, bell-like snap (*Ta / Tini*).

### The Soul of Kirtan & Baul
The Khol is designed to induce ecstatic devotional tempo accelerations (*Dohar / Jhulan*). Its signature technique is **Krena**—a two-finger sliding flourish on the right head that gives Bengali rhythms their swinging lilt.

---

# Mridangam Studio Specification (`readme_Mridangam.md`)
======================================================
## The King of Percussion in Carnatic Classical Music
**Instrument:** Mridangam / Kappi Mridangam (South Indian Carnatic Barrel Drum)  
**Traditions:** Carnatic Concerts, Harikatha, Bharatanatyam, Temple Melams  
**Tuning Class:** Chromatic Melodic Classical (Tuned strictly to Katcheri $Sa / Shruti$)  
**Standard Bank / Preset:** Bank 42 Presets 0–11 (Tuned Sa=C..B), Preset 116 (Sa=C#) | GM Kit: Bank 128 Preset 120  
**Multi-Velocity Layers:** 3 Tiers (Soft `0-60`, Medium `61-110`, Hard `111-127`)

---

## 1. Instrument Physics & Acoustic Character
The Mridangam is the premier rhythmic foundation of Carnatic music.
* **Valamthalai (Right Head):** Crafted from three concentric rings of layered hide. At its core is the **Karanai (Soru)**, a permanent paste made of iron slag powder, boiled rice, and tamarind juice, polished with river stone. When struck properly, it vibrates in **pure mathematical harmonics (a singing fifth)**, creating the bell-like *Chapu* and *Dheem*.
* **Thoppi (Left Head):** Larger head loaded with a temporary moist paste of cream of wheat (rava) and water. Provides a warm, loose, resonant boom (*Dheem*) and allows the left wrist to modulate acoustic tension during the stroke to produce **Gumki** (pitch-sliding bass).

---

# Pakhawaj Studio Specification (`readme_Pakhawaj.md`)
======================================================
## Majestic Classical Percussion of Ancient India (Dhrupad & Haveli Sangeet)
**Instrument:** Pakhawaj / Mridang (North Indian Classical Barrel Drum)  
**Traditions:** Dhrupad, Dhamar, Haveli Sangeet, Temple Kathak, Classical Indian Dance  
**Tuning Class:** Chromatic Melodic Classical (Tuned to Performer's Tonic $Sa$)  
**Standard Bank / Preset:** Bank 44 Presets 0–11 (Tuned Sa=C..B), Preset 116 (Sa=C#) | GM Kit: Bank 128 Preset 119  
**Multi-Velocity Layers:** 3 Tiers (Soft `0-60`, Medium `61-110`, Hard `111-127`)

---

## 1. Instrument Physics & Acoustic Character
The Pakhawaj is the grand ancestor of the Hindustani rhythm family.
* **Left Head (Dhumma / Bass):** Prepared fresh for every concert with **wet wheat-flour dough (*aata*)** applied to the center. This adds massive physical weight to the skin without raising stiffness, creating an immense, subsonic, room-shaking bass boom (*Dhumma / Ge*) devoid of high sliding meends.
* **Right Head (Dayān / Treble):** Larger and heavier than a Tabla Dayan, featuring a wide permanent black *syahi*. Struck with full-hand weight and open palms, producing deep, authoritative, noble resonance (*Din, Ta, Tit, Chhapa*).

### Aesthetic Role
Pakhawaj music is architectural, mathematical, and spiritual. It accompanies the solemn microtonal movements of the Rudra Veena, Surbahar, and Dhrupad vocalists.

---

## 3. Idiomatic Patterns for AI Arrangers

### A. Classic 12-Matra Chautaal (Dhrupad Benchmark)

# Kanjeera & Ghatam Studio Specification (`readme_Kanjeera_Ghatam.md`)
======================================================================
## Carnatic Secondary Percussion & Upapakkavadyam Ensembles
**Instruments:** Kanjeera (Lizard-Skin Frame Drum) & Ghatam (Baked Clay Pot)  
**Traditions:** Carnatic Classical, Thani Avarthanam (Drum Duels), Fusion, World Percussion  
**Tuning Class:** Kanjeera (Unpitched with Dynamic Pitch-Bends) | Ghatam (Tuned Clay Chamber)  
**Standard Banks:** Kanjeera (Bank 45) | Ghatam (Bank 46)  

---

## 1. Kanjeera Architecture (Bank 45 Preset 121)
The Kanjeera is a small round frame drum made of jackfruit wood ($7	ext{ inches}$) with a single head of monitor-lizard skin and two small brass jingles.
* **The Magic of Gumki:** The left holding hand moistens the inner skin with water droplets and modulates wrist/finger pressure to bend notes up to a fifth, producing soaring vocal-like bass pitch glides.

### Kanjeera Note Map (MIDI Notes 36 – 73)
| MIDI Note | Key Name | Bol / Stroke | Role | Acoustic Character |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|---|
| **36** | C2 | **Tom / Dheem** | Bass | Open resonant frame drum bass tone |
| **39** | D#2 | **Gumki (Slide)** | Bass | Moist heel pressure glide bending pitch upwards |
| **42** | F#2 | **DimPr (Mute)** | Bass | Holding fingers damping skin for staccato bass |
| **48** | C3 | **Ta (Rim Slap)** | Treble | Crisp edge slap with frame body resonance |
| **50** | D3 | **Me (Singing Bell)**| Treble | Resonant sweet tone on open skin |
| **52** | E3 | **Ki (Staccato Tap)**| Treble | Dry staccato tap for fast Korvai subdivisions |
| **57** | A3 | **Ta Sharp** | Treble | High-velocity rim snap |
| **72** | C5 | **Jingle Clash 1** | Auxiliary | Direct brass coin clash |
| **73** | C#5 | **Jingle Clash 2** | Auxiliary | Alternate frame jingle vibration |

---

## 2. Ghatam Architecture (Bank 46 Preset 122)
The Ghatam is a heavy clay pot baked with copper, brass, and iron filings. It is played with fingers, thumbs, palms, and fingernails.
* **Mouth Pop (Ghumki):** Striking the open palm flat against the pot mouth creates a vacuum pop with deep cavernous resonance.
* **Shoulder & Belly:** Struck with finger rings and knuckles, producing ringing metallic overtones.

# Indian Folk & Auxiliary Percussion Specification (`readme_Folk_Auxiliary.md`)
================================================================================
## Regional Drums, Bells, Cymbals & Traditional Idiophones
**Instruments:** Naal, Punjabi Dhol, Duff / Daphli, Tavil, Ghunghroo, Khartaal, Nagara, Chimta, Manjeera  
**Traditions:** Bhangra, Lavani, Garba, Temple Melams, Sufi Qawwali, Rajasthani Folk  
**Standard Bank:** Bank 47 | GM Kit: Bank 128 Preset 123  

---

## 1. Instrument Highlights & Sound Palette

### A. Naal (Filmi & Lavani Drum)
A cylindrical wooden drum bridging Dholak and Tabla. Features a screw-tuned high-tension Dayan head with syahi mounted on a Dholak body. Crisp, tight, and punchy.

### B. Punjabi Dhol (Bhangra King)
A massive two-headed barrel drum played with wooden sticks: **Dagga** (thick curved bass stick) and **Tilli** (thin flexible treble cane). The heartbeat of Punjabi celebrations.

### C. Traditional Idiophones & Bells
* **Ghunghroo (Notes 74–75):** Brass ankle bells tied with cotton cord; essential for Kathak, Bharatanatyam, and ghazal rhythmic shimmers.
* **Khartaal (Notes 76–77):** Handheld wooden clappers with small cymbals, providing the galloping tempo of Rajasthani folk and devotional bhajans.
* **Nagara (Notes 78–79):** Massive kettledrums played with sticks for ceremonial and royal fanfare.
* **Manjeera (Notes 69–70):** Heavy cast-bronze cymbals with silvery sustain.
* **Chimta (Note 71):** Iron fire-tongs fitted with brass jingle clusters, famous in Punjabi folk and Qawwali.

---
